finding.claim: The authorization check on DELETE /reports/:id is async but is not awaited. Its 403 rejection is never observed, so any authenticated user can delete any report. The rejected promise also becomes an unhandled rejection, which can crash newer Node versions.
finding.source: Any authenticated user sends DELETE /reports/<id> for a report they have no 'delete' grant on. The id comes from req.params.id.

trace.note: The report is fetched by the attacker-supplied id.
authorize(...) is called without await or return, so the handler continues immediately.
authorize is async. Its throw at line 14 becomes a rejected promise that nobody handles.
db.reports.remove runs regardless of the grant result.
The handler returns 204, so the attacker sees success.

finding.guards_checked: authorize() is correct in itself, and the PUT handler at line 27 awaits it. The DELETE handler has no await, no .then or .catch, and no other middleware that checks permissions. The only global middleware, at lines 4-7, sets req.user and does no authorization.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at server.js:9-16 throws a 403 on a missing grant, but the DELETE handler discards the returned promise (line 20). The only global middleware (lines 4-7) sets req.user and does no authorization.
verdict.reason: server.js:20 calls async authorize() as a bare statement without await, so its throw at line 14 never stops db.reports.remove at line 21 or the 204 at line 22. The PUT handler awaits it at line 27, so a low-privilege authenticated user can delete any report, and the rejection goes unhandled.

finding.claim: The PUT /reports/:id handler passes the whole client-supplied JSON body to db.reports.update. A user with write access can therefore overwrite protected fields such as owner, id or tenant. Whether this is exploitable depends on db.reports.update, which is not in the repo.
finding.source: A user with 'write' permission sends a JSON body to PUT /reports/:id, including fields like owner_id, id or tenant_id.

trace.note: The authorize check only verifies the 'write' action on the report. It does not restrict which fields may be written.
The raw body goes to update with no field allowlist.

finding.guards_checked: There is no schema validation or field allowlist in this file. The db layer is not present, so any filtering inside update could not be checked. That is why this is a lower-confidence candidate.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at server.js:9-16 is awaited at line 27 and throws a 403 on failure, so it effectively gates the write action, but it does no field filtering. No schema validation or allowlist exists in server.js. db is not defined in the repo, so any filtering inside db.reports.update cannot be checked.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: server.js:3 parses the body, server.js:27 awaits authorize for 'write' only, and server.js:28 passes the raw req.body to db.reports.update. Whether protected fields such as owner or id can be overwritten depends on db.reports.update, which is not in the repo. The attacker would be an authenticated user who already has 'write' on the report.
